prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a rare case where a quantitative prediction preceded a decisive experiment. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of 2011 located the magic angle and the flat bands; the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity by Jarillo-Herrero's group confirmed that a single tunable parameter could drive strongly correlated electrons. From my own vantage in electronic-structure theory, what stands out is that a simple band-structure idea turned out to control many-body physics, and that the field has since reproduced the phases in many groups and many moire systems. That breadth and originality, and the clean theory-plus-experiment split into three names, make it the strongest candidate on my list.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity. The pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated ground states are still debated, the field is only about seven or eight years past the experimental discovery, and the supplied names leave out Yuan Cao and the parallel experimental work of other groups. A prize now would honour the discovery of the platform rather than a settled understanding, and the committee has historically preferred to wait when the interpretation is moving. If the committee holds that line, the lattice clock is the safer and more mature choice.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B035 sixth and calls the physics not yet stable and perhaps slightly premature, because the origin of the superconductivity and the correlated states remains debated.
responses.response: I take the point seriously but I would separate the discovery from its explanation. The claim to be rewarded is the prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and the experimental demonstration that they host correlated insulators and superconductivity. Both are independently reproduced and are not in dispute; the mechanism is open, but we have honoured discoveries before the mechanism was understood. Where I concede ground is on the citation, which should be worded narrowly on the platform and phases and make no claim about the pairing mechanism.

responses.point: Lindroth puts the optical lattice clock first as an original, mature, well-confirmed invention, and judges the magic-wavelength physics sound from the atomic-structure side.
responses.response: I agree that B008 is mature, cleanly attributed in two names and has the strongest opening support, and I ranked it fifth rather than lower for that reason. My disagreement is about scientific weight. Beyond a large gain in precision, I do not see in it a change in how we understand matter comparable to a new tunable platform for strongly correlated electrons. I also share the worry that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize have already covered adjacent ground. I would regard it as an entirely defensible prize, and my first alternative, rather than my first choice.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the aberration-corrected electron microscope first and notes that Cao and other junior experimenters, and Krivanek on STEM correction, fall outside the supplied names, which is a real attribution question.
responses.response: I agree on the substance of the attribution problem for both entries, and the Cao point applies to my own first choice. I think the cases differ in that the three-name configuration for B035 follows the prediction-plus-discovery structure that the committee has accepted before, whereas B009 has a competing independent STEM-corrector line that the three names cannot cover. I do give B009 real weight, since aberration correction underpins atomic-resolution work on magnetic and two-dimensional materials that I rely on, and I have placed it as my second alternative. I would resist describing it as mere instrumentation, but I would not move it ahead of a discovery with this much downstream physics.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and flags both his proximity to the field and the question of whether it is sufficiently separate from the 2025 prize.
responses.response: His openly stated bias is the right way to handle the proximity. As Chair for the 2025 cycle I would add that the 2025 prize concerned macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in circuits, so circuit QED can be argued to be distinct, but a follow-up so soon in the same hardware family would be a hard case to make. That is why I have not placed B012 in my configuration, though it is scientifically strong.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene need not be settled before a prize.
Whether the three supplied names fairly cover the experimental discovery given Yuan Cao and the parallel graphene experiments of other groups.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize and the 2010 graphene prize make the committee reluctant to reward another graphene-based or band-topology result so soon.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: none of the credited persons for B035, B008 or B009 is a documented collaborator, supervisor or Uppsala colleague. I note only that I chaired the 2025 cycle, which bears on how I weigh circuit QED (B012), and that my own field of electronic-structure and 2D materials theory is adjacent to B035, which I treat as a bias to discount.
